title: Experiencing school history in apartheid and post-apartheid South Africa: an autoethnographic study of historical and transactional distances
abstract: This autoethnographic study explores the complexities of experiencing school history education in apartheid and post-apartheid South Africa, highlighting the tensions between curriculum content and pedagogical delivery. Drawing on the personal experiences of the first author as a learner during the transition from apartheid to democracy, and later as a history education lecturer, the article contrasts apartheid-era memory history – characterised by a singular nationalist narrative promoting white supremacist ideologies – with contemporary analytical history, which emphasises historical thinking, critical enquiry, human rights and democratic engagement. The theoretical lenses of transactional and historical distances provide a conceptual framework to understand these educational experiences, illustrating how historical narratives and teaching methodologies influence learner engagement. Methodologically, the study employs autoethnography, utilising personal memories, historical documents and reflective practice to unpack the educational transitions experienced by the first author. Findings indicate that despite curriculum reforms aiming to promote analytical history, traditional peda

title: Teaching history and the climate crisis: missed opportunities in Finnish textbooks?
abstract: Amid escalating ecological disruptions, history education holds significant value in helping students to make sense of our present predicaments and future projections. This article examines how Finnish secondary-level history textbooks engage with the climate crisis, one of the most pressing concerns of our time. Through qualitative content analysis, nine digital textbooks were analysed to assess both the prevalence and framing of the phenomenon, particularly in relation to industrial societies, drawing on the concepts of climate justice and multispecies justice. Of interest was whether textbook narratives foster historical thinking – the core aim of history curricula – to provide students with access to subject-specific powerful knowledge on the climate crisis. The findings suggest that Finnish history textbooks often overlook crucial opportunities to develop historically grounded, as well as socially and ethically nuanced, knowledge of the phenomenon, perhaps highlighting a need for more explicit integration of the climate crisis into history curricula.

title: The Holocaust and AI testimony: repackaging the past in the digital age
abstract: This article examines the use of artificial intelligence testimony in Holocaust remembrance as survivors age and their numbers dwindle, and focuses on Reverberations: An AI Powered Exhibition at the Sydney Jewish Museum, Australia. Preserving eyewitness accounts is crucial for history, education, refuting denial and the promotion of reflection. The exhibition uses artificial intelligence technologies to create interactive conversations with survivors and a multimedia theatre experience exploring key themes. Using a model based on four domains – History Disciplinary Practices, Metahistorical Concepts, Past/Present (Dis)juncture and Popular Culture and Theatre – and data from researchers and pre-service history teachers, the study analyses the audience experience. Findings indicate that the Metahistorical Concepts domain scored highest in both exhibition formats, suggesting effectiveness in fostering critical understanding of ‘big picture’ historical ideas. Survivor conversations driven by artificial intelligence were more effective in creating personal connections and building empathy through micro-narratives and interactive dialogue, while the Theatre Experience provided more insti

title: Rethinking historical consciousness under ideological education: master narratives, institutional evaluation and marginal effects in China
abstract: This article examines the marginal effects of ideological control in history education by comparing the master narratives embedded in Chinese high school history textbooks with the interpretations offered by 29 first-year university students who completed their secondary education in China. Despite the growing body of research on history education and ideology, there remains limited empirical work on how state-sponsored historical narratives are actually interpreted by students. In this article, we treat textbooks as a form of hegemonic memory apparatus and analyse the extent to which this hegemonic memory is reproduced, adapted or questioned by learners. Our findings are threefold. First, the textbooks construct modern Chinese history primarily through a humiliation narrative and a rejuvenation mission narrative, which emphasise the moral superiority and historical role of the Chinese Communist Party. Second, students show strong emotional engagement with these narratives but do not fully internalise the class-based and stereotyped historical judgements presented in the text. Third, when ideological control is intensified and historical conclusions replace detailed accounts, stude

title: ‘Doing history teaching with GenAI’: an exploration of teaching practices during an AI pilot project in Germany
abstract: Although teachers’ actions are considered central to history lessons, little is known about their teaching practices with regard to the use of generative artificial intelligence. In this article, we ask which teaching practices were carried out among teachers in history lessons while using generative artificial intelligence in a pilot project at German schools with schulKI (schoolAI). To this end, we analysed interviews with and project documentation from 12 history teachers who took part in the pilot project. Based on considerations from practice theory and a socio-cultural view of history education, we analysed our data sources and identified four central teaching practices that characterise ‘doing history teaching with GenAI’: (a) obtaining support from generative artificial intelligence for the preparation of history lessons; (b) introducing practices of utilising generative artificial intelligence in history lessons; (c) integrating generative artificial intelligence into the implementation of history lessons; and (d) managing with situational demands through the use of generative artificial intelligence in history lessons. In this article, we present our praxeological observa

title: ‘I never thought history could be told this way’: exploring teachers’ use of comics in history education
abstract: This article examines how comics can enhance history education by challenging traditional, text-centred approaches to historical knowledge. Despite growing interest in visual culture, historical scholarship and pedagogy often continue to privilege written texts as more legitimate sources of knowledge. Drawing on focus group interviews with history educators from Sweden, Türkiye and the United States, this article explores how teachers utilise comics in classroom settings and what pedagogical value they attribute to them. The research reveals that comics can serve as powerful tools for fostering historical thinking, empathy and engagement, especially through their ability to present complex, layered narratives that resist linear storytelling.

title: Talent development in history education
abstract: This article investigates the development of historical curiosity and career interest among professional historians. Using a mixed-methods approach, including a survey (n = 163) and focus groups (n = 10), we examine when and how individuals become interested in history as a profession. Findings indicate that while historical curiosity can emerge in early childhood, significant career interest typically develops during undergraduate and graduate education. Key factors influencing this development include engaging history courses, internships, independent reading and mentorship from professors and professionals. The article reveals a progression of influential experiences from elementary school through early career, with formal education and practical experiences becoming increasingly important in later stages. Family influence and early exposure to historical content also play significant roles. The research highlights the need for a multifaceted approach to fostering historical interest, combining structured educational experiences with opportunities for self-directed exploration and real-world application of historical skills throughout an individual’s educational and professional

title: Inclusion through pluralisation? European history teachers’ beliefs on inclusion
abstract: Understanding teachers’ beliefs as a set of views that guide their work with students, this article explores selected European history teachers’ beliefs on inclusion in history education. The article considers inclusion as a concept and a policy that has gained increased attention, while its definition and practical implementation have not been unified or systematic. With the aim of better understanding the beliefs of European history teachers on inclusion in history education, this article analyses focus group interviews with 18 participants. Thematic analysis of the focus group interview data was conducted using a set of codes, which resulted in three themes: who history teachers considered as the recipients of inclusion; what problems and benefits history teachers linked to inclusion and history teaching; and the content and practice of inclusion in history education described by the history teachers. First, the results show that the history teachers define various groups that need to be considered in the context of inclusion, although students with special educational needs are most frequently mentioned as the addressees of inclusion. Second, the article indicates that history

title: The politics of writing and teaching secondary school history in independent Zimbabwe: silenced voices in textbooks and the classroom
abstract: In tracing Zimbabwe’s history of liberation, which culminated in the independence of 1980, there are individuals, families, communities and other sections of society which are deemed to have undermined the armed struggle, whether this is real or perceived. Such people include those who joined Rhodesian Security Forces and Rhodesia’s militias, such as Security Force Auxiliaries, District Security Assistants, Guard Force and Shangaan Army. The list also encompasses Africans behind attacks on refugee and guerrilla camps in Mozambique, Zambia and Angola, anyone who sided with Rhodesians and people who got punished by guerrillas, allegedly for selling out. The article focuses on silenced politicians and their political parties who lost the 1980 elections because they take centre stage in the history which is publicly remembered and taught in schools. The main objective of this article is to explore ways in which such people are side-lined in the history of the liberation struggle through an examination of the history curriculum in Zimbabwe’s secondary schools. This contribution is useful in widening the understanding of how history is taught, preserved and written after a protracted arm

title: The co-curation of collective memory: artificial intelligence, Holocaust survivor testimony and the contribution of museum educators
abstract: Holocaust survivor testimony is increasingly being preserved using emerging technologies in preparation for a post-survivor era. A key approach to this process is exemplified by the Dimensions in Testimony platform developed by the University of Southern California Shoah Foundation, which involves the utilisation of natural language-processing artificial intelligence to facilitate interactive, language-driven experiences with specially filmed testimony. Alongside receiving praise for its authentic representation and participatory capabilities, this approach has given rise to ethical debates about how oral testimonies can be preserved, since there are some elements of human experiences that defy translation into digital media. In this article, we address the research question: how can museum educators work with interactive video testimonies to generate historical consciousness? The contribution that we aim to make is to broaden and clarify the scope for future human–artificial intelligence interactions in this context by elaborating on the expressions of historical consciousness that were embedded in perspectives of museum educators at the Sydney Jewish Museum. Interviews took place

title: Historical perspective taking in primary school history textbooks
abstract: This article examines how two widely used Dutch primary school history textbooks promote historical perspective taking. Historical perspective taking refers to the mental activity of attempting to take the perspective of historical people. In this article, we use a dual conceptualisation of historical perspective taking, comprising historical contextualisation and perspective taking. History textbooks are important in the way history lessons are designed in primary schools because of non-expert teachers’ tendency to follow the textbook. Our corpus of analysis consisted of the textbooks’ tasks, texts and teacher guides. The results showed that textbooks promoted different approaches to historical perspective taking, sometimes leaning more towards a discipline-specific approach of historical perspective taking, including knowledge of the historical context, the use of sources and chronology, with others sometimes leaning towards a more generic approach of historical perspective taking, including imagination about historical people’s perspectives. These different approaches of historical perspective taking in history textbooks foster different educational goals. Awareness of these dif

title: Promoting historical reasoning in inquiry-based history education: design of a professional development programme
abstract: Many primary school teachers consider history to be a challenging subject to teach. In this educational design study, we developed a professional development programme for primary school teachers, aimed at enhancing their pedagogical content knowledge and skills for designing inquiry-based history lessons that foster pupils’ historical reasoning. In the first cycle we formulated aims and design principles and developed a prototype programme based on teacher interviews and literature on effective teacher professional development, historical reasoning and inquiry-based learning. The programme was subsequently piloted with four teachers in grades 3–6 (pupils aged 8–12 years old) in the Netherlands. We developed a coding scheme to analyse professional growth during the programme. In the second cycle we revised principles and the professional development programme based on key findings of the pilot. These findings indicate that collaborative inquiry activities and modelling historical reasoning triggered personal change. We designed lessons based on classroom observations and pupils’ feedback to support the development of practice. Moreover, searching for and discussing sources and thei

title: Digital déjà vus: an investigation into how AI image generators s(t)imulate historical thinking
abstract: This exploratory study investigates the capacity of AI image generators to produce historically coherent visualisations and evaluates their didactic potential. In 2024, 1,024 images generated from six leading models were analysed using a standardised visual content analysis tool across four dimensions: historical significance, epochal authenticity, comparative lifeworld depiction and archetypal representation. The findings indicate that, while the output adequately depicts epochal atmospheres, it lacks concrete historical referents and exhibits poor independent historical judgement. Archetypal hero motifs predominantly emerged in medieval and classical guises, thereby reinforcing Western iconography. Only one model produced largely recognisable events and comprehensible comparisons through automated prompt augmentation, despite still reproducing biased historical narratives and stereotypes. The results highlight the potential of AI image generators to confront students with various conceptual problems, biases and anachronisms that can be discussed in class to encourage historical thinking. The study calls for didactic frameworks that integrate AI-generated images into structured hi

title: History education in historical perspective: editorial
The process of historical questioning: a systematic literature review
abstract: The majority of history educators in the English- and German-speaking contexts concur that the objective of history education is to foster historical thinking. While there exist some models for the progression of second-order concepts that provide an analytical framework to support these learning processes, such models are almost entirely lacking for the procedural aspects of historical thinking. This is also true for historical questioning, which is generally regarded in the literature as the ‘engine’ of historical thinking. However, there remains a paucity of theories and empirical studies that systematically operationalise the process of historical questioning and its development. To address this research gap, our systematic literature review provides in-depth insight into relevant studies on (historical) questioning from different angles in order to conceptualise three main operations of historical questioning: (1) experiencing perplexity, (2) expliciting perplexity and (3) expressing the historical question. Furthermore, the review systematises sub-operations and quality characteristics of both the process of historical questioning and its operations. Finally, the results are

title: Why think historically when AI can do it? Understanding the relationship between generative artificial intelligence and history teacher identity
abstract: The advent of generative artificial intelligence technologies that can create high-level texts effectively mimicking historical thinking has raised critical questions for history educators. While much of the existing literature related to history education and generative artificial intelligence has studied history teachers’ need to develop skills to keep up with the new technology, this article seeks to understand history teachers’ perspectives concerning their purpose and their profession in relation to generative artificial intelligence. Drawing on interviews with history teachers in British Columbia, Canada, this article demonstrates the ways in which the introduction of generative artificial intelligence created conditions of significant uncertainty for history teachers and the ways teachers’ self-understandings were renegotiated under these conditions. Participants’ perspectives ranged from promoting the need to ‘leverage’ historical thinking to understand generative artificial intelligence, to finding a renewed sense of purpose in helping students ‘think along the way’, to building students’ human capacities to defend against techno-capitalism. Rather than indicating an end t

title: Theorising intergenerational trauma through the prism of history-in-the-now: historical consciousness, the sense-making process and its potentials for self-transformation
abstract: This article theorises the relationship between intergenerational trauma and historical consciousness, seeking to understand how negatively impregnated experiences of traumatising events that people inherit and interiorise can be actualised in their sense-making as a form of possibility for renewal and strength. Such an examination, which investigates how inheritors of collective trauma view history’s workings and how these understandings shape their social positioning, can provide much-needed insight into the historical knowledge that inheritors bring to formal history classrooms and the different strategies that can be adopted to help them (and others) overcome these traumatic events’ negative imposition on their self-identity and ability to act positively in the world. The article particularly focuses on the notion of inheritors’ transgenerational atmosphere that holds them captive to the limiting experiences of their predecessors’ lived horrors, as they relate to the concept of history-in-the-now, which offers a novel way of grasping the workings of historical consciousness. Moreover, the author’s broader practical life methodology is introduced as a pedagogical approach to hel

title: ‘My Friend! you and I have passed our Lives, in Serious Times’: undergraduate reflections on the purpose of studying history
abstract: In the summer of 1813, John Adams wrote to Thomas Jefferson, saying, ‘you and I have passed our Lives, in Serious Times’. History has guided past generations and remains a crucial tool for helping students understand the present through the study of the past. In the United States, recent decades have shown a degree of growing indifference towards history in college and university curricula, suggesting that the value of history might be diminishing. This qualitative study explored 103 undergraduate student essays from a state college in the southeastern United States on ‘Why study history?’ using four guiding questions: (1) How does the study of history help us in our everyday lives? (2) How does history help us better understand ourselves and the world around us? (3) What purpose does the study of history have in the college curriculum today, if any? (4) How does history prepare us to be active citizens in our community? The McNeill–Stearns framework guided data analysis and two cycles of coding. A range of themes were generated through the first cycle of coding and refined in the second cycle. The following four themes – prepare for the future, repeating history, lessons of histor

title: Working on democratic memory through Spanish history textbooks: how far do they contribute to developing competences for a democratic culture?
abstract: This article aims to explore how teaching the evolution of twentieth-century democracy in Spanish history textbooks contributes to the promotion of competences for a democratic culture of learners. The textual content and types of activities proposed in five different textbooks used in the fourth year of compulsory secondary education in Spain were analysed to shed light on how teaching about ‘democratic memory’ may contribute to the understanding of democracy of learners. The findings suggest that although the transmission of a narrative articulated around the democratisation process of the country is present in all textbooks, and many of the activities suggested in the books help to enhance students’ understanding of democracy, there is still work to be done regarding the training of historical thinking skills that help learners understand how more plural and inclusive narratives of the past may be constructed.

title: Epistemic rhythms in lesson assignments: exploring the interplay of diverse content and objectives in teaching materials on historical and contemporary societal issues
abstract: This article examines the design of lesson assignments addressing historical and contemporary societal issues in schools, with particular emphasis on the knowledge content required to respond to the questions posed in these assignments. The aim is to investigate the didactic functions that can be identified in school lesson assignments that elicit various types of knowledge. Two research questions are posed: (1) What epistemic positions can be identified in school lesson assignments? (2) What epistemic rhythms between different selections of knowledge can be identified in school lesson assignments? The methodology used involves a text analysis of 124 lesson assignments provided by 10 upper secondary teachers. The results identify three primary epistemic rhythms in the lesson assignments, which are the movements between student-oriented, context-oriented and analysis-oriented knowledge. These correspond in different ways to the didactic functions of broadening, reorganisation and evaluation. An overarching conclusion is that teachers’ approaches to designing lesson assignments with varying epistemic rhythms can serve as a means to address diverse educational objectives and reflect t

title: ‘It has so much history behind it, for such a small place’: exploring place-based, interdisciplinary and community-driven approaches to teaching local history in the Young Voices project, Southall
abstract: The Young Voices project supported primary and secondary school children across Southall, West London, to learn about the unique local history of the town, in particular its history of migration and anti-racist activism. This reflective article explores the project’s community driven, place-based and interdisciplinary approach to teaching local history, highlighting the use of local community spaces and material cultures as sites for learning. In the 2023/24 school year, history and visual art workshops were delivered collaboratively, predominantly to Year 6 (key stage 2) and 7 (key stage 3) children, both in classrooms and at local sites, by local community charity Southall Community Alliance, anti-racism organisation The Monitoring Group and a visual artist and lecturer from Central Saint Martins, University of the Arts London. The workshops focused on the experiences of migrant communities in the 1960s and 1970s, exploring pivotal events of the time, such as the murder of Gurdip Singh Chaggar, the Southall Uprising and the death of Blair Peach. On 23 April 2024, marking the anniversary of the 1979 anti-racism demonstration, all artworks and the project film were displayed at a m

title: Pedagogical approaches for climate justice orientations to teaching history and social studies
abstract: In this article we address the question: what is a climate justice approach to teaching history and social studies? Building from history education literature on the topic of climate history, we review international literature in climate change education and climate justice education published between 2017 and 2023 to develop conceptions of climate justice education relevant to teaching history and social studies more specifically. We customised 11 themes derived from the literature review as pedagogical prompts for history and social studies teachers. Our purpose is to offer teachers an overview of research-informed pedagogical approaches from which they can select as they determine the needs and strengths of their learners, and as they consider the kind of climate justice educator they hope to be in a history or social studies classroom.

title: A material perspective on pupils’ experience during museum education as a space for historical consciousness
abstract: This article investigates pupils’ experience with historical objects during an educational visit to a history museum and how this can foster the development of historical consciousness. It is investigated from the pupils’ perspective, which is done by using a theoretical frame consisting of a relational ontological understanding of the pupil, a cultural pedagogical understanding of historical consciousness and an understanding of the experience with museum materiality as an oscillation between meaning effect and presence effects. The article draws on data from 287 pupils (aged 12–16 years) visiting Rosenborg Castle. This was collected through a material and collaborative ethnographic approach, employing qualitative cartographic observations, dialogical sticky note exercises and qualitative photo-elicited surveys, in collaboration with 10 museum professionals all affiliated with museum education from Rosenborg Castle, The Workers Museum, National Museum of Denmark, Museum of Copenhagen and Skoletjenesten. The article offers insights into the richness and complexity of pupils’ material experiences and historical consciousness during museum education. It concludes by highlighting that

title: Shaping historical consciousness: young people, social remembering and identity dynamics outside the classroom
abstract: This article explores how young people’s engagement with history outside the classroom shapes the development of their historical consciousness. The findings are drawn from a two-year doctoral research project investigating the social remembering of young people from England during the 100-year commemoration of the First World War. Building on recent work by Peck and Zanazanian, and foundational insights from Hall and Epstein, the article explores how young people’s historical consciousness is shaped through their self-positioning within national, racialised and cultural frameworks. Complementing this, I draw on Samuel and Wertsch to conceptualise history and memory as socially embedded practices, often located in vernacular, familial and community spaces outside formal education. These perspectives come together in the concept of social remembering, which captures how young people actively construct historical meaning through relational, affective and culturally situated engagements with the past. As Thelen argues, such remembering is not fixed but dynamic, constantly worked and reworked. This research draws on ethnographic work with a small group of students to address the resear

title: Agent ontologies and the history classroom: a more-than-human experiment
abstract: There is a case to be made for a more-than-human experiment for history education that challenges the inside/outside of the history classroom by expanding our understanding of the past beyond the limits of the human-centred, historical past. This more-than-human experiment can be realised by bringing agent ontologies into conversation with historical thinking. Agent ontologies are philosophical positions where humans are not the apex of existence and agency is not seen as something only humans have. It is the position of this article that certain assumptions to do with time, distance and the concept of the human frame the inside of the history classroom and, to truly overcome the inside/outside binary, where anything outside is seen as other, it is necessary to develop ontological positions that challenge these assumptions. Two more-than-human concepts, the history-student-in-place and historical affect, are outlined to provide tangible and theoretically sound ways for history educators to adapt their teaching practices. title: Orientation in time and world through history and civic education: curricular frameworks and teachers’ perspectives in Austria
abstract: This article explores the connection between historical and political learning as well as their contribution to the promotion of democratic consciousness in Austrian lower secondary education. The analysis is based on the assumption that students need not only historical orientation skills but also competence in political judgement and political action to develop into historically critical, mature citizens. Against this background, the Austrian curriculum for the combined subject of History and Civic Education at the lower secondary education level was categorised historically and examined for points of reference regarding the promotion of democratic consciousness. Using the deductively derived categories of democracy, orientation and maturity, the article finds that while the curriculum refers to democratic values and human rights as an overarching goal, historical and political competences are not consistently linked. In addition, it includes teachers’ perspectives on the subject combination of history and civic education and their teaching and learning objectives. The analysis of 43 expert interviews shows that the combination of subjects is mainly considered from the perspectiv

title: Putting the past in place: meetings with local archives in history education
abstract: This study investigates how an intervention in place-based history education can be planned and implemented by history teachers and staff from cultural heritage institutions at a local archive. Through a single case study, the planning, implementation and post-processing of the participating teachers and heritage actors are analysed using interviews and observations. The results show that place-based history education can link history education with the resources of cultural heritage institutions, such as archives, and can promote local history. Logistical challenges for teachers constitute significant obstacles to collaboration between schools and cultural heritage institutions, while school digitisation policies limit the use of physical sources in history education. The study also reveals that experienced teachers adapt place-based history education differently based on their teaching strategies and motivations, with an eclectic teaching strategy being especially fruitful for collaborations with different actors within place-based history education. The research highlights the potential of place-based history education to enhance collaboration, revealing shared goals and fosteri

title: A vote for Australian democratic consciousness: teaching civics through history
abstract: This article aims to contribute a framework for how historical consciousness can be guided by moral consciousness. It argues that through adopting a goal of cultivating democratic consciousness and implementing a dynamic pedagogy, teachers and students can meaningfully engage with mis- and disinformation to challenge the suppositions they bring with them. These approaches work against the virulent effects of misinformation, which was a prime factor in the failure of Australia’s Referendum on the Voice to Parliament, as well as national elections in 2024 which produced victories for authoritarian or populist candidates. The first section briefly reviews how the descriptions of Civics and Citizenship Education have shifted in Australian curricula, from the issue of the Hobart Declaration (1989) to the present, to respond to cultural and social developments. A second section examines the key challenges and opportunities for democratic renewal, particularly in relation to how teachers can instruct students to plan for effective political participation at school so as to more authentically engage with their communities. This focus includes what can be learned from the ineffectiveness of

title: Never the two shall meet? Connecting historical and democratic consciousness in Canadian K-12 history textbooks
abstract: This article explores the intersections of historical and democratic consciousness in education, drawing on data from a study of history textbooks in Canada. We conducted a holistic analysis of 18 history textbooks published between 1994 and 2021, authorised for use at the elementary/middle school or secondary level in each provincial jurisdiction within Canada. The findings demonstrate that while many textbooks make assumptions that knowing more about the past leads to the creation of better citizens, historical and democratic consciousness are not fully developed and are largely disconnected from one another. We also found significant differences in the presence and articulation of historical and democratic consciousness between the oldest and more recently published textbooks, with more recent textbooks engaging with history in ways that promote the development of both historical and democratic consciousness. If we are to support students in becoming historically informed civic leaders in the present and into the future, we argue that all history textbooks authorised for use in Canada must pay greater attention to the connections between historical and democratic consciousness.

title: Poetry as a site of history education and exploration: learning history from and with poetry
abstract: Poetry has, historically and currently, been used to express resistance against hegemonic powers and power abuses. Poems have the potential to be both historical sources and personal comments on history, containing historical content and framing this content in a narrative. Poetry can also be useful in teaching difficult and painful histories, bringing emotions to the forefront of historical engagement. This article argues that poetry can be a powerful site of history education and exploration outside formal education spaces, using both published poems and student poetry writing exercises. It argues that poetry can be a site of history education through finding and exploring historical and existing poetry, and that poetry can be a site of history exploration through students writing poetry themselves. Poetry presents a way to explore voices of resistance and marginalised voices on their own terms, in an emotive expression that nevertheless carries historical argument. Writing poetry can bring students into contact with history in a different way, where they are in touch either with the histories that have affected and shaped them, or with history interpreted from their own viewpoin

title: Can a constructivist, community-based intervention increase student motivation to study history? A case study from Ghana
abstract: Student interest in studying history is in decline in Ghana, as it is in secondary schools in many other parts of the world. Can student interest be stimulated, and can they be better served, by a curriculum that includes a focus on community, belonging and co-creation? This article details a preliminary intervention of just such a learning unit in a high school in Central Region, Ghana. Using a framework aligned with the historically responsive literacy approach, this programme supported student-directed research into aspects of local and personal history. The evidence from this study suggests that student motivation did increase, justifying an expanded future study of greater length, with additional participants, and building on the lessons from this preliminary effort.

title: The Great Irish Famine in Irish and UK history textbooks, 2010–2020
abstract: This article considers the representation of the controversial issue of the Great Irish Famine (1845–50) in 27 recent Irish and UK history textbooks for the secondary level. Key contested issues – imports and exports, the British government’s laissez-faire economic policy, providentialist interpretations, and victim–perpetrator discourses – have long formed part of the narrative repertoire of Famine history; their representation and narrativisation in textbooks is analysed through narrative and content analysis. Historical contextualisation and perspective taking are considered key skills for students studying history; these skills become even more important when dealing with controversial issues. The questions central to this research are: How do secondary-level history textbooks from Ireland and the UK represent the key contested elements regarding the Famine? Do they provide sufficiently complex accounts, thereby facilitating historical contextualisation and perspective taking? While some Irish and UK textbooks offer learners complex representations of the Famine, several others provide students with insufficient opportunity for perspective taking, and for developing a thorough

title: Unthinking historical thinking: lessons from the Arctic
abstract: In a 2017 book chapter on the continuing erasure of Indigenous epistemes in academia, the Sami scholar Rauna Kuokkanen posed an important question: is it acceptable for a site of learning to be so ignorant? Foregrounding Indigenous scholarship from the Arctic, this article examines the potential of history education to address this question. Based on previous research on Arctic gender history and the coloniality of knowledge, I suggest a paradigm shift, in view of the new UNESCO Education for Sustainable Development framework (May 2021). The research investigates the challenges and opportunities that history education offers in terms of epistemic and cognitive justice within the context of Arctic memory cultures. The article concludes that much can be learned from (not about) Indigenous scholarship, which has long demonstrated a range of critical and sustainable methodologies that offer opportunities to seek epistemic justice and the restitution of cultural memory.

title: Controversial issues and the nature of history: Teachers’ views on controversial historical issues in Swedish lower secondary school
abstract: Controversial issues are often regarded as abundant in history education. Most topics can be regarded as controversial in one way or another. The purpose of this article is to analyse the way history teachers in Swedish lower secondary schools relate controversial issues to a particular view of the nature of the subject of history. By analysing statements from six teacher interviews which centred on the risks and opportunities associated with teaching about controversial issues, the authors were able to see a clear relation between views on controversial issues and views on the nature of history as such. The teachers’ reactions to the introduction of controversial issues, whether introduced by the teacher or by the students, was in many cases directly related to a specific view of the subject itself and its epistemological nature.

title: Not by the book: the teaching of history in Norwegian kindergartens
abstract: This article reports a local study of the presence of history as a subject in the kindergartens of Kristiansand, a municipality in southern Norway. There is no syllabus for history in the national curriculum; nevertheless, the research sought to find historical content in the kindergartens. The research method was informed by a precept of history didactics, namely that history is everywhere. Using this observation, tentative categories for content likely to feature history were formulated, and then searched for in the individual yearly plans of the kindergartens. This was supplemented by interviews. It is concluded that, in accordance with the national curriculum, history in the kindergartens is a local affair. It emerges especially through local history, visits to museums, and projects with historical features. This research was not designed to determine whether learning outcomes in history are achieved, nor to consider kindergartens outside Kristiansand. However, it references a corpus of literature on history in Norwegian kindergartens, and interacts with it. The conclusion about the presence of the subject is the same as was found for another city, Trondheim, in research by oth

title: A systematic review of pedagogical interventions on the learning of historical literacy in schools
abstract: Over the past thirty years, there has been a growing body of research investigating the efficacy of pedagogical interventions to enhance the historical literacy skills of primary and secondary school students. However, there exists no systematic review or meta-analysis summarising the impact of such research or the efficacy of interventions trialled. The purpose of this systematic review is to identify pedagogies that have a demonstrable effect on students’ historical literacy skills, with a particular interest in those pedagogies that have a measurable positive effect on historical epistemological knowledge and skills. Findings of this review indicate that when a discrete historical epistemological knowledge or skill is targeted by a pedagogical intervention that utilises a discipline-specific scaffolded heuristic, there is greater likelihood of positive outcomes for student learning. However, the significant heterogeneity between studies, and the diversity in the comparisons being made by the included studies, make it difficult to identify the most effective intervention. This systematic review establishes the characteristic features of pedagogical historical literacy interventio

title: Investigating subject-specific writing skills and historical reasoning in historical explanations: a study of 7th- and 8th-grade comprehensive school students in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine the writing skills of 7th- and 8th-grade students with a high proportion of migration background in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. The study was part of the SchriFT project (2017–20), funded by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research. A writing task was given on the topic: Why can we only make assumptions about many past events? As an answer to the task, the students had to write a historical explanation that took into account the epistemological principles of historical reasoning. The students’ writing was analysed using a category system, and their historical knowledge was assessed through a knowledge test. The results showed that the students possess diverse levels of writing skills, with few producing elaborate explanations, and most struggling with the subject-specific language and reasoning skills. The study also highlights the potential for genre-based writing approaches in history education. The results suggest that many students perceive history as an image of the past and have limited understanding of historical reasoning. title: Educational reforms and teaching of history in contemporary Spain – nation, history and education as contested issue
abstract: This article analyses the changes in education legislation and the history curriculum in Spain over recent decades. To this end, the characteristics established for the teaching of history in the last two education laws, passed in 2013 and 2020 – the first by a conservative government and the second by a progressive one – are studied and compared. This study is carried out by situating the education debates presented in this research in the social and political context of Spain. The study of these legislative changes allows us to observe the different visions of national identity existing in Spain, which find a prominent area of confrontation in education and the teaching of history. The article also argues that the emergence of the ultra-right has led to a markedly nationalist vision of Spanish history that seeks to recover elements of national unity, and that has become one of the axes defended by conservative options for the teaching of history in Spanish schools. This view contrasts with the approaches advocated in the latest education legislation, which propose a more heterogeneous approach to the subject of identity in Spain.

title: Exploring differential effects of an intervention on historical inquiry tasks: a qualitative analysis of 12th-grade students’ progress
abstract: Multiple-documents-based (inquiry) tasks are often used to examine historical thinking, as they require students to apply discipline-specific ways of reasoning and writing. Intervention studies using such tasks have often relied on principles from cognitive apprenticeship to make these discipline-specific heuristics explicit to students. While several studies have found positive results, they offer little insight into how and where exactly students’ progress on historical thinking manifests itself, nor into the differential effects of the intervention. Building on essay data gathered during an intervention study on students’ historical inquiry skills, this study explores differential effects of the intervention according to students’ initial historical inquiry ability. To this end, a purposeful sample of students was selected for whom the intervention was particularly effective. The qualitative analysis of students’ essay tasks (pretest and posttest) revealed remarkable differences between students with high and low pretest scores. title: Whose story should we be telling? An exploration of student attitudes towards, and perceptions of, the British history curriculum
abstract: Amid a growing national debate regarding the current health and future direction of the history curriculum in Britain, there have been numerous calls for an examination of its roles and purposes, and questions have been raised as to how far it engages an increasingly diverse student body. This article examines the perceptions and attitudes of students towards the history curriculum within the context of one secondary school in south-east England through an exploratory case study. The findings draw upon research undertaken with Year 9 students, through 105 completed questionnaires, and through focus group interviews conducted with 12 participants. Thematic analysis suggests that, although students very much value learning about British history, they would prefer a curriculum with a wider focus which incorporates broader global studies. Although the environment offered by the case study is not particularly socially diverse, there is evidence that some groups of students desire greater curriculum reform and inclusivity. title: Re-enactment, resilience and regression in Türkiye’s history education: a post-postcolonial analysis
abstract: This article examines Türkiye’s history education from the Cold War to the present, tracing a shift from postcolonial imagination to a post-postcolonial configuration. Combining close readings of history textbooks with insights from the scholarly literature, it shows how historical re-enactment functions as a political technique that stabilises postcolonial imagination. The post-postcolonial argument centres on a dual transformation: drawing on Partha Chatterjee’s distinction between the spiritual and material domains, it preserves yet radicalises the postcolonial spiritual domain (faith, morality, civilisational belonging) while re-coding the material domain (science, economic development, technology, modernisation) through anti-Western and anti-scientific narratives. Within this framework, the 2024 Century of Türkiye Education Model History curriculum serves as a recent manifestation of these dynamics.
